title: Adjective Complements: Infinitives, -ing and Clauses
summary: Select adjective complements after linking verbs, including to-infinitives, -ing forms, that-clauses and wh-clauses. Control the meanings of particular adjectives and use anticipatory it and it makes someone structures accurately.
learningObjectives: Choose appropriate complements for common and advanced adjective patterns, respecting restrictions on individual adjectives.
Distinguish infinitival action, -ing activity and finite that- or wh-clauses where their grammatical roles differ.
Recast subject-first descriptions as anticipatory it + adjective + to-infinitive or clause and select of for personal evaluations.
Use it made someone + adjective + complement to report reactions and avoid replacing the adjective with an unrelated verb pattern.

explanation.heading: Adjectives license different complements
explanation.body: After a linking verb, the complement depends on the adjective. Ready, willing and reluctant commonly take to-infinitives; busy takes an -ing form directly; worried and confident may introduce that-clauses; and uncertain or unsure can introduce wh-clauses such as whether or why. Some adjectives allow more than one pattern, but not necessarily with the same meaning. A dictionary entry for the adjective is more reliable than a universal rule.
explanation.example: The team is ready to begin, but its coordinator is unsure whether the equipment has arrived.

explanation.heading: To-infinitive, -ing and finite clauses do different jobs
explanation.body: A to-infinitive often names an action someone is willing, able or likely to perform: eager to contribute. An -ing form can describe an activity accompanying an adjective: busy preparing a speech. A that-clause adds a full proposition: pleased that the results improved. A wh-clause conveys unresolved information: uncertain how the change happened. In some contexts that is optional, but whether and how cannot simply be dropped without changing the structure.
explanation.example: The designer was busy drafting alternatives and pleased that the team supported her.

explanation.heading: The same adjective may admit more than one pattern
explanation.body: Adjectives including foolish and stupid can take either to-infinitives or -ing clauses when assessing an action, although the framing may differ. Afraid can take a to-infinitive to describe reluctance to perform an action or a that-clause to express worry about a proposition. With feel, adjectives such as guilty and awful frequently precede -ing or a that-clause. Keep the meaning and subject relationship clear instead of replacing complements mechanically.
explanation.example: He was afraid to ask a question because he was afraid that the answer would be negative.

explanation.heading: Anticipatory it shifts focus away from long subjects
explanation.body: A long infinitival subject can often be moved to the end with introductory it: To interpret the chart was difficult becomes It was difficult to interpret the chart. Adjectives can also be followed by wh- or that-clauses, as in It is unclear why the signal disappeared. With adjectives evaluating someone’s conduct, of + person is often natural: It was thoughtful of her to call. For ability, ease and difficulty, for + person commonly identifies who experiences the task: It was difficult for us to follow.
explanation.example: It was generous of the organiser to provide free tickets.

explanation.heading: It made someone + adjective describes a reaction
explanation.body: To report an emotional response, use it + made + object + adjective, often with a following to-infinitive, -ing clause or that-clause: It made me nervous to speak first. The object is the person who felt the emotion, and the adjective characterises that reaction. This differs from make someone do something, where the bare infinitive names an action caused by another person. Do not combine the two constructions indiscriminately.
explanation.example: It made her happy to hear that the exhibition had succeeded.

left.label: Adjective + to-infinitive
left.example: The panel was willing to reconsider.
left.note: Willing expresses readiness to take the action named by the infinitive.

right.label: Adjective + that-clause
right.example: The panel was certain that the figures were correct.
right.note: Certain introduces a complete proposition believed to be true.

comparisons.title: Of someone and for someone after anticipatory it

left.label: It + adjective + of a person
left.example: It was considerate of Leo to reply promptly.

right.label: It + adjective + for a person
right.example: It was difficult for Leo to reply promptly.
right.note: Difficult evaluates the task’s difficulty for Leo, not his character.

examples.sentence: The volunteers were ready to help when the visitors arrived.
examples.note: Ready is followed by a to-infinitive naming the intended action.

examples.sentence: The curator was busy cataloguing the new donations.
The residents were pleased that the road had reopened.
examples.note: Pleased introduces the proposition giving the reason for the feeling.

examples.sentence: The supervisor was unsure why the schedule had changed.
examples.note: A wh-clause identifies the unresolved information.

examples.sentence: It was kind of the technician to stay late.
examples.note: The anticipatory it construction uses of to evaluate the technician’s behaviour.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The committee was willing reconsider the proposal.
commonMistakes.correct: The committee was willing to reconsider the proposal.
commonMistakes.why: Willing selects a to-infinitive; the marker to cannot be omitted.

commonMistakes.incorrect: She was busy to organise the exhibition.
commonMistakes.correct: She was busy organising the exhibition.
commonMistakes.why: Busy takes an -ing clause describing the ongoing activity.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We were uncertain that did the warning appear.
commonMistakes.correct: We were uncertain why the warning appeared.
commonMistakes.why: An embedded wh-clause follows normal statement word order without did-support; why expresses the unanswered question.

commonMistakes.incorrect: It was generous for Nina to share her notes.
commonMistakes.correct: It was generous of Nina to share her notes.
commonMistakes.why: In this assessment of Nina’s generosity, of Nina is the standard pattern.

studyTips: Create an adjective-pattern notebook: enter willing to, busy -ing, pleased that and uncertain whether with full sentences.
Transform an infinitival subject into it + be + adjective + infinitive, then distinguish of from for by asking whether you evaluate a person or a task.
Contrast afraid to act with afraid that something might happen, and read both aloud with a realistic situation.

exercises.prompt: The employees are ___ the new procedure after the training session. Choose the complete natural adjective phrase.
exercises.feedback: Ready licenses a to-infinitive: ready to follow.

exercises.prompt: During the exhibition, the curator was ___ the new collection.
exercises.feedback: Busy is followed directly by an -ing form describing the activity.

exercises.prompt: The manager cannot explain the reason for the delay. Which complement expresses that uncertainty?
choices: unsure why did the delay occur
unsure to why the delay occurred
exercises.feedback: An embedded why-clause retains statement order: why the delay occurred.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence evaluates a person’s kindness rather than how difficult the action was?
choices: It was hard of Maya to help the visitor.
It was kind for Maya to help the visitor.
It was kind of Maya to help the visitor.
exercises.feedback: Kind of Maya evaluates her personal conduct; for is usual with difficulty adjectives.

exercises.prompt: The musicians were eager ___ perform at the opening. Supply the infinitive marker.
acceptedAnswers: to
exercises.feedback: Eager is followed by a to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: The assistants were busy ___ (prepare) the seating plan. Supply the -ing form.
acceptedAnswers: preparing

exercises.prompt: The scientist was unsure ___ the readings had changed. Supply the interrogative word meaning for what reason.
acceptedAnswers: why
exercises.feedback: Why introduces the embedded question about the reason.

exercises.prompt: It was thoughtful ___ Tom to send the revised timetable. Supply of or for as appropriate.
acceptedAnswers: of
exercises.feedback: Thoughtful evaluates Tom’s considerate behaviour, so use of.

exercises.prompt: Correct the complete sentence: The hosts were pleased that the visitors had arrive early.
acceptedAnswers: The hosts were pleased that the visitors had arrived early.
exercises.feedback: The past perfect requires had + past participle, arrived; the that-clause supplies the full proposition.

exercises.prompt: Correct the complete sentence: She was busy to pack the exhibition crates.
acceptedAnswers: She was busy packing the exhibition crates.
exercises.feedback: Busy takes the -ing complement packing, not to pack.

exercises.prompt: Correct the complete sentence: It was generous for the neighbour to offer a ride.
acceptedAnswers: It was generous of the neighbour to offer a ride.
exercises.feedback: Generous evaluates the neighbour’s conduct, so of is appropriate.

exercises.prompt: Correct the complete sentence: They were uncertain where should they meet.
acceptedAnswers: They were uncertain where they should meet.
exercises.feedback: Embedded wh-clauses use statement word order: where they should meet.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use a to-infinitive after ready. Facts: We / be / ready / to begin. Use the present simple.
acceptedAnswers: We are ready to begin.
speakingExercises.feedback: Ready to begin uses the required infinitive form.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use busy with an -ing complement. Facts: The staff / be / busy / preparing dinner. Use the past simple.
acceptedAnswers: The staff were busy preparing dinner.
The staff was busy preparing dinner.
speakingExercises.feedback: Busy preparing describes the ongoing activity; both agreement patterns occur with collective staff.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give one complete sentence beginning "She was pleased" and ending "the proposal had passed." Use an explicit that-clause.
acceptedAnswers: She was pleased that the proposal had passed.
speakingExercises.feedback: That introduces the proposition causing her pleasure.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use an embedded question. Facts: I / am / unsure / whether / the door is locked.
acceptedAnswers: I am unsure whether the door is locked.
I’m unsure whether the door is locked.

speakingExercises.prompt: Evaluate personal generosity. Say exactly: "It was generous of Eva to share her notes."
acceptedAnswers: It was generous of Eva to share her notes.
speakingExercises.feedback: Generous of Eva evaluates her character and action.

speakingExercises.prompt: State a task difficulty for someone. Facts: It / difficult / for us / to reach the venue. Use past simple.
acceptedAnswers: It was difficult for us to reach the venue.
speakingExercises.feedback: Difficult for us describes the task’s difficulty for the group.

speakingExercises.prompt: Contrast two meanings of afraid. Say these sentences in order: "He was afraid to complain." Then "He was afraid that nobody would listen."
acceptedAnswers: He was afraid to complain. He was afraid that nobody would listen.
speakingExercises.feedback: The infinitive describes reluctance to act; the that-clause expresses worry about an outcome.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe an emotional reaction with make. Facts: It / made / me / happy / to see them. Use past simple.
acceptedAnswers: It made me happy to see them.
speakingExercises.feedback: Made me happy reports a feeling produced by seeing them.

listeningExercises.audioText: By ten o’clock, the team was ready to begin the demonstration in the main hall.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was the team ready to do?
listeningExercises.feedback: Ready to begin names the intended action.

listeningExercises.audioText: The assistant was busy preparing the guest list all afternoon and could not answer the phone.
listeningExercises.prompt: What occupied the assistant during the afternoon?
listeningExercises.feedback: Busy preparing is the adjective-plus--ing pattern used in the audio.

listeningExercises.audioText: The director was unsure whether the meeting would continue after lunch.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the exact two-word phrase describing the director’s certainty.
acceptedAnswers: unsure whether
listeningExercises.feedback: Unsure whether introduces an unresolved yes-or-no issue.

listeningExercises.audioText: It was considerate of Omar to offer his seat to the visitor who was using a walking stick.
listeningExercises.prompt: How did the speaker evaluate Omar’s action?
listeningExercises.feedback: Considerate of him evaluates Omar’s conduct.

listeningExercises.audioText: The room was noisy, so it was difficult for the visitors to understand the announcement.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was difficult for the visitors?
listeningExercises.feedback: It was difficult for the visitors to understand the announcement.

listeningExercises.audioText: I was afraid that the train would be late, so I called the reception desk.
choices: The schedule had already been revised
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker was afraid that the train would be late, which is worry about a proposition.

listeningExercises.audioText: It made me nervous to speak first, but everyone responded kindly.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the exact three-word phrase describing the speaker’s emotion.
acceptedAnswers: made me nervous
listeningExercises.feedback: Made me nervous expresses the speaker’s resulting feeling.

listeningExercises.audioText: The volunteers were pleased that the repairs had finished ahead of schedule.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the exact two-word phrase describing the group’s feelings.
acceptedAnswers: pleased that
listeningExercises.feedback: Pleased that introduces the complete proposition explaining the group’s happiness.
